analysis.one_liner: Requires a full government audit of the Federal Reserve and a report to Congress.
analysis.headline: A bill requiring a full government audit of the Federal Reserve drew 320 House cosponsors — every Republican and a majority of Democrats — but never got a committee vote or a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the Government Accountability Office, Congress's investigative arm, to complete a full audit of the Federal Reserve's Board of Governors and all twelve regional Reserve banks before the end of 2010, then send a detailed report of its findings to Congress. It would strike the limits Congress wrote in 1978 that currently exempt the Fed's monetary policy operations and its transactions with foreign central banks from that audit. In short, it would let an independent auditor look at parts of the Fed that no outside auditor can see today.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and ordinary people who want to know how trillions of dollars in crisis-era lending and monetary operations were handled. Members of Congress would get the audit findings and any Member could request the report, giving lawmakers facts they currently cannot obtain about the Fed's emergency lending, its dealings with foreign central banks, and how its decisions were made.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers seeking visibility into the Fed

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Comptroller General (the head of the GAO) to complete an audit of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors and the federal reserve banks before the end of 2010, followed by a detailed report to Congress with findings and recommendations.
Amends the audit law by striking the current limits, so the GAO audit would cover the Fed's monetary policy operations and other activities that are exempt from GAO review under the 1978 framework.

Requires the audit report to be delivered to House and Senate leaders, the committees of jurisdiction, and any other Member of Congress who requests it, putting the findings in the hands of all 535 lawmakers rather than a small set of officials.

analysis.who_pays: The Federal Reserve itself, which would lose the audit exemptions it has operated under since 1978 and face public congressional scrutiny of its dealings, and the banks and financial institutions that received Fed emergency lending, whose names, terms, and conditions could surface in the audit report.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Federal Reserve and aided banks

drawbacks.text: The bill would remove the 1978 exemptions that shield the Fed's monetary policy deliberations and its transactions with foreign central banks from GAO audit, so critics warned that opening rate-setting deliberations to congressional auditors could subject interest-rate decisions to political pressure and uncertainty in markets.

The bill mandated a one-time audit and a single report due by the end of 2010, with no standing requirement for recurring audits afterward, so its transparency value depended heavily on what that one report chose to examine.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — an independent, published accounting of how the Fed managed trillions of dollars during the financial crisis — was real and inexpensive, and most serious objections were about precedent rather than the audit itself. The bill's weakness was design: a single mandatory report with no follow-on audit schedule limited how much lasting transparency it would create. On balance, the transparency gains outweighed the political-pressure concern, and the bill posed no direct cost to taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, got a single hearing, and died there without ever being voted on by the committee or the full House.

narrative.text: Ron Paul introduced the Federal Reserve Transparency Act of 2009 in the House on February 26, 2009, and it was referred to the Committee on Financial Services.
The bill drew 320 cosponsors — all 178 House Republicans and 142 of 253 House Democrats — a supermajority of the chamber.
The Financial Services Committee held a hearing on September 25, 2009, the only committee action of substance the bill ever received.
The committee never reported the bill, and the House never voted on it; it expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Federal Reserve kept its audit exemptions, and the banks that benefited from its emergency lending avoided having those arrangements detailed in a public report to Congress. (Congress later required a limited one-time GAO audit of the Fed's crisis lending through the 2010 Dodd-Frank law, but the full audit this bill demanded was never enacted.)

sides.party_line_note: Support was unusually bipartisan: all 178 House Republicans and 142 of 253 House Democrats — 320 of 431 members — cosponsored, yet the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill would end the Fed's exemptions from GAO audit of its monetary policy operations and dealings with foreign central banks, and require a published report on its conduct. The Fed's institutional interest in keeping those operations shielded from outside audit runs directly against the public's interest in knowing how its crisis lending was handled.

Banks that received Fed emergency lending during the financial crisis could have their identities, terms, and conditions disclosed in the audit report. That exposure serves the public's interest in accountability but works against the banks' preference for confidentiality.
